title: Tunnel magnetoresistance effect with a Cr-doped $\mathrm{RuO_{2}}(110)$ altermagnet
authors: Katsuhiro Tanaka, Takuya Nomoto, Ryotaro Arita
abstract: Antiferromagnets can have a finite spin-polarization in the momentum space when their magnetic structure breaks the macroscopic time-reversal symmetry. This spin-polarization can produce a spin-polarized electric current even in antiferromagnets with vanishingly small net magnetizaton, which supports the antiferromagentic tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) effect. In this paper, using first-principles calculations, we study the TMR effect with a doped altermagnet $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}$ with $(110)$ orientation, whose collinear antiferromagnetic structure breaks the time-reversal symmetry macroscopically. The momentum-dependent spin-polarization combined with the $(110)$ crystal orientation makes the electric current spin-polarized through bulk $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$. We further calculate the TMR effect in the $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)/\mathrm{TiO_{2}}(110)/\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$ tunnel junction and show that a finite TMR effect emerges. Based on the analysis of the tunneling transport, the TMR effect is attributed to the spin polarized tunneling transport with momentum dependence and the interfacial magnetic structures, as well as the spin-polarized electric current in a bulk form of $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_{x}\mathrm{O}_{2}(110)$.
summary: This theoretical study calculates the Tunnel Magnetoresistance (TMR) effect in a doped altermagnet $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_x\mathrm{O}_2(110)$ junction. Using DFT, the authors demonstrate that a finite TMR signal emerges due to spin polarization originating from the crystal structure and interfacial effects. This work advances understanding of spintronics in antiferromagnetic oxides.
main_problem: The study investigates the Tunnel Magnetoresistance (TMR) effect occurring in antiferromagnetic tunnel junctions using doped altermagnets.
main_result: A finite TMR effect is predicted and calculated for $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_x\mathrm{O}_2(110)/\mathrm{TiO}_2(110)/\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_x\mathrm{O}_2(110)$ junctions, attributed to momentum-dependent spin polarization and interfacial magnetic structures.
method: The research employs first-principles calculations (DFT) combined with the scattering theory method and Landauer–Büttiker formalism to model tunneling transport.
model_or_system: The system is a Magnetic Tunnel Junction (MTJ) composed of $\mathrm{Ru}_{1-x}\mathrm{Cr}_x\mathrm{O}_2(110)$ altermagnets separated by a $\mathrm{TiO}_2(110)$ barrier. The material properties are derived from first-principles calculations using the virtual crystal approximation for Cr doping.
key_observables: Total spin polarization ($p_{	ext{tot}}$), momentum-dependent spin polarization $p(\mathbf{k}_{\parallel})$, total transmission ($\mathrm{T}_{	ext{P}}, \mathrm{T}_{	ext{AP}}$), and the TMR ratio.
important_parameters: Cr doping concentration ($x$), crystal orientation ($(110)$ vs $(001)$), and Fermi energy ($E_{	ext{F}}$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the TMR effect arises from a combination of bulk spin-polarized current, momentum dependence, and interfacial magnetic structures.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structures for different orientations, show how total spin polarization changes with Cr concentration, map out the momentum dependence of spin polarization, and plot the calculated TMR ratio versus doping concentration and barrier thickness.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical basis by showing that the $(110)$ orientation allows for a finite bulk spin-polarization in the altermagnet. It then applies this to model the MTJ structure, calculating the TMR effect based on tunneling transport theory and analyzing its dependence on doping and barrier thickness.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter magnetism, the calculation of electronic transport properties (TMR) using first-principles methods is foundational for understanding quantum phenomena in solid-state devices, which has parallels with open quantum system modeling.
